title: Two Saudi Emirates
subtitle: 1744–1900 · The First Saudi State, the Egyptian Destruction, the Second State and the Rise of the Āl Rashīd

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: Two Saudi states rise and fall in Najd — the First conquering most of Arabia before Egypt razes Dirʿiyya, the Second a smaller emirate torn apart by a ten-year succession war and finished off by the Āl Rashīd of Ḥāʾil

entries.group: The First Saudi State — the Emirate of Dirʿiyya (1744–1818)
entries.label: Muḥammad ibn Saʿūd and the consolidation
entries.hint: With the shaykh's doctrine as banner and the alms-tax and war booty as engine, the amīr of Dirʿiyya spent twenty years bringing the towns of Wadi Ḥanīfa under his rule — the small beginning of the first pan-Arabian state since the Caliphate.
entries.note: Ibn Bishr, ʿUnwan al-majd fi taʾrikh Najd; Madawi Al-Rasheed, 'A History of Saudi Arabia' (2010).

entries.group: The First Saudi State — the Emirate of Dirʿiyya (1744–1818)
entries.label: ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn Muḥammad and the great expansion
entries.hint: He conquered Riyadh after a thirty-year war with Dahhām ibn Dawwās, then al-Qaṣīm, then al-Aḥsāʾ in 1795 — ending the Banū Khālid — and raided into Iraq and the Hijaz. He was assassinated in the Dirʿiyya mosque in 1803 by a Shiʿi avenger of Karbala.
entries.note: Ibn Bishr; Ibn Ghannām, Rawḍat al-afkar.

entries.group: The First Saudi State — the Emirate of Dirʿiyya (1744–1818)
entries.label: Saʿūd al-Kabīr and the height
entries.hint: Saʿūd 'the Great' took Mecca in 1803 and Medina in 1805, expelled the Ottoman-appointed sharif, imposed Wahhābī practice on the Holy Cities, and refused the Egyptian and Syrian Hajj caravans. The state reached from Iraq to Oman and from Yemen to the edge of Syria.
entries.note: Ibn Bishr; J. L. Burckhardt, 'Notes on the Bedouins and Wahábys' (1830).

entries.group: The First Saudi State — the Emirate of Dirʿiyya (1744–1818)
entries.label: ʿAbd Allāh ibn Saʿūd, the last of Dirʿiyya
entries.hint: He inherited a state already under Egyptian attack, fought the long retreat through the Hijaz and Najd, and after a months-long siege surrendered Dirʿiyya in September 1818. He was sent to Istanbul and beheaded.
entries.note: Ibn Bishr; the Egyptian campaign accounts; George Sadleir, 'Diary of a Journey across Arabia' (1866, for 1819).

entries.label: Ibrāhīm Pasha and the Egyptian occupation
entries.hint: On the sultan's order, Muḥammad ʿAlī of Egypt sent his son Ṭūsūn to retake the Hijaz (1812–13) and then his son Ibrāhīm Pasha to grind through Najd (1816–18). The Egyptians razed Dirʿiyya, garrisoned the interior, and pulled out in 1824 under tribal resistance and cost.
entries.note: the Egyptian sources on the Arabian campaign; Burckhardt (1830); ʿAbd al-Raḥīm ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, 'al-Dawla al-Suʿūdiyya al-ūlā'.

entries.group: The Second Saudi State — the Emirate of Najd (1824–1891)
entries.label: Turkī ibn ʿAbd Allāh and the refounding
entries.hint: A survivor of the dynasty retook Riyadh in 1824 and made it the new capital — Dirʿiyya was left in ruins — rebuilding a smaller Saudi state over Najd and al-Aḥsāʾ. He was assassinated by a cousin in 1834.
entries.note: Ibn Bishr, ʿUnwan al-majd; Al-Rasheed (2010).

entries.group: The Second Saudi State — the Emirate of Najd (1824–1891)
entries.label: Fayṣal ibn Turkī, the central reign
entries.hint: The defining ruler of the Second State: deposed and taken to Cairo by a second Egyptian invasion in 1838, he escaped in 1843, retook Riyadh, and ruled for twenty-two more years over a stable emirate that levied tribute from the Gulf coast as far as Oman.
entries.note: Ibn Bishr; Lewis Pelly, 'Report on a Journey to the Wahabee Capital of Riyadh' (1866); R. Bayly Winder, 'Saudi Arabia in the Nineteenth Century' (1965).

entries.group: The Saudi Civil War and the Rashīdī Ascendancy (1865–1900)
entries.label: The Saudi civil war
entries.hint: Fayṣal's sons ʿAbd Allāh and Saʿūd fought for the throne for a decade; Riyadh changed hands again and again and the state consumed itself. While the Saudis fought each other, the Ottomans retook al-Aḥsāʾ in 1871 and never gave it back.
entries.note: Ibn Bishr's continuators; Winder (1965); the Ottoman records of the 1871 al-Aḥsāʾ expedition (Midhat Pasha).

entries.group: The Saudi Civil War and the Rashīdī Ascendancy (1865–1900)
entries.label: Muḥammad ibn Rashīd of Ḥāʾil
entries.hint: The amīr of Jabal Shammar, an Ottoman client, exploited the Saudi civil war — took al-Qaṣīm, defeated the Saudi coalition at Mulayda in 1891, occupied Riyadh, and ruled all of Najd from Ḥāʾil. Contemporaries called him Muḥammad the Great.
entries.note: Charles Doughty, 'Travels in Arabia Deserta' (1888); Wilfrid and Anne Blunt, 'A Pilgrimage to Nejd' (1881); Al-Rasheed, 'Politics in an Arabian Oasis: The Rashidis of Saudi Arabia' (1991).

entries.group: The Saudi Civil War and the Rashīdī Ascendancy (1865–1900)
entries.label: The Saudis in exile
entries.loc: the Rubʿ al-Khali, Qatar, Bahrain and Kuwait
entries.hint: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Fayṣal and his family — including his son ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz — fled Riyadh after Mulayda: into the desert with the Āl Murra, then to Qatar and Bahrain, and from 1893 to Kuwait under Mubārak Āl Ṣabāḥ. The dynasty's third exile.
entries.note: H. St John Philby, 'Saudi Arabia' (1955); Al-Rasheed (2010); the Kuwait years covered in the memoirs of ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz's circle.

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: Fifty years of conquest, the sack of Karbala and the taking of the Holy Cities, the Egyptian war that destroyed the First State, a second Egyptian invasion, and the Battle of Mulayda

entries.group: The Wars of the First State
entries.label: The conquest of Najd
entries.hint: Fifty years of town-by-town war — the thirty-year reduction of Riyadh, the taking of al-Qaṣīm, and finally al-Aḥsāʾ in 1795 — turned a one-town emirate into the ruler of the interior and its coasts.
entries.note: Ibn Bishr, ʿUnwan al-majd, whose annals record the campaigns year by year.

entries.group: The Wars of the First State
entries.label: The sack of Karbala
entries.hint: A Saudi-Wahhābī force stormed the Shiʿi shrine city, destroyed the tomb of Ḥusayn, and killed several thousand people. The raid sent a shock through the Shiʿi world and the Ottoman empire and turned the Saudi state into a target that had to be dealt with.
entries.note: the Ottoman and Iraqi Shiʿi accounts; Juan Cole, 'Sacred Space and Holy War' (2002). The death toll is an estimate and is disputed.

entries.group: The Wars of the First State
entries.label: The taking of the Holy Cities
entries.hint: Mecca fell in 1803 and Medina in 1805; the domes over the graves of the Baqīʿ cemetery were demolished, the Ottoman Hajj was refused entry, and the sultan's claim to protect the Ḥaramayn was directly and publicly challenged.
entries.note: Burckhardt, 'Notes on the Bedouins and Wahábys' (1830); the sharifian chronicles.

entries.label: The siege and destruction of Dirʿiyya
entries.hint: Ibrāhīm Pasha's advance through Najd with field and siege artillery the Saudis could not answer culminated in a six-month siege of Dirʿiyya. The town fell in September 1818 and was deliberately levelled and its palm groves cut down.
entries.note: the Egyptian campaign records; Sadleir, who reached Ibrāhīm's camp in 1819; Burckhardt (1830).

entries.label: The second Egyptian invasion
entries.hint: Muḥammad ʿAlī sent Khurshīd Pasha back into Najd, capturing Fayṣal and installing a client amīr, before the whole Egyptian position in Arabia collapsed with Muḥammad ʿAlī's defeat by the European powers in 1840 and the withdrawal from the Levant.
entries.note: Winder, 'Saudi Arabia in the Nineteenth Century' (1965).

entries.label: The Battle of Mulayda
entries.hint: Muḥammad ibn Rashīd decisively defeated the Saudi and Qaṣīmi coalition near Buraydah, then occupied Riyadh. The Āl Saʿūd fled the capital, ending the Second Saudi State after sixty-seven years.
entries.note: Al-Rasheed, 'Politics in an Arabian Oasis' (1991); the Qaṣīmi and Rashīdī accounts.

entries.label: Khuwa, ghazw and the tribute wars
entries.hint: Under both states the everyday military work was the raid, the forced collection of zakāt-as-tribute from reluctant tribes and towns, and the punitive column. It was the same low war as ever, now waged in the name of a state and a doctrine.
entries.note: Ibn Bishr; the ethnographic accounts of Najdi raiding (Doughty, Musil).

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: A war-state that ran on booty, a theology turned into a police system, the Second State's chastened pragmatism, and the succession problem neither state solved

entries.label: Zakāt, ghanīma and the war-state
entries.hint: The First State ran on the alms-tax of submitted districts and the fifth of the plunder from its raids. Conquest paid for conquest. When Saʿūd al-Kabīr's expansion reached its limit, the revenue base did too — just as Egypt attacked.
entries.note: Ibn Bishr; the analysis of the First State's fiscal base in ʿAbd al-Raḥīm ʿAbd al-Raḥmān and in Al-Rasheed (2010).

entries.label: The doctrine as state law
entries.hint: The Āl al-Shaykh and the qāḍī corps enforced the Wahhābī sharīʿa — the demolition of shrines, the ban on tobacco, music and the mourning rites, the mutawwiʿa sent to make towns pray. A theology became a legal and police system.
entries.note: Ibn Ghannām; Guido Steinberg, 'Religion und Staat in Saudi-Arabien' (2002); Michael Cook on the enforcement.

entries.label: The Second State's pragmatism
entries.hint: Turkī and Fayṣal ran a smaller, more cautious emirate — no more assaults on the Ḥaramayn, a working accommodation with the Ottomans and the British, a softer enforcement. It was Wahhābism adapted to a state that had already been destroyed once.
entries.note: Winder (1965); Pelly's 1865 report on Fayṣal's government.

entries.label: The succession problem
entries.hint: Neither state fixed how to pass power. The First State's amīrs mostly managed it; but ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz and Turkī were both assassinated, and Fayṣal's death set off a ten-year civil war that let Ḥāʾil in. The lack of a rule is the structural flaw of both.
entries.note: Al-Rasheed (2010); Joseph Kostiner on Saudi state formation.

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: The doctrine acquires an army and a treasury, the war on the shrines becomes state policy, the wider Muslim world's condemnation hardens, and enforced practice remakes public religion in Najd

entries.label: Wahhābism as the ideology of a state
entries.hint: For the first time the doctrine had an army and a treasury behind it. The 'call' became a reason for war, and submission to the Saudi amīr and acceptance of the doctrine were made a single act — a fusion of religion and state that has never come apart.
entries.note: Steinberg (2002); DeLong-Bas, 'Wahhabi Islam' (2004).

entries.label: Takfīr and the war on the shrines
entries.hint: The practical programme: declaring shrine-venerating Muslims unbelievers whose blood and property were licit, and systematically demolishing the tombs and domes of Najd, Karbala and the Ḥaramayn. It is what turned a doctrine into a casus belli against most of the Muslim world.
entries.note: Ibn Ghannām on the demolitions; Cook, 'On the Origins of Wahhābism' (1992).

entries.label: The wider Muslim condemnation
entries.hint: The Ottoman ʿulamāʾ, the Shiʿi authorities, the Sufi orders and the sharifian Hijaz all condemned the movement. The fatwās and the counter-histories that began with the First State shaped how the Muslim world saw the Saudi project for two centuries.
entries.note: the Ottoman refutations; the Iraqi Shiʿi accounts of Karbala; Samer Traboulsi and Ahmad Dallal on the early anti-Wahhābī literature.

entries.label: Enforced practice and its limits
entries.hint: The mutawwiʿa, compulsory mosque attendance, the burning of tobacco and the smashing of instruments genuinely transformed public religious life in Najd — but the chronicles and the travellers also record how partial, resisted and reversible that transformation often was.
entries.note: Doughty's observations at Ḥāʾil; Steinberg (2002); the Najdi chronicle notices of backsliding.

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: At-Turaif built and then dynamited, the plainer Riyadh of the Second State, the suppression of music and image, and the war-poetry the state did encourage

entries.label: At-Turaif and the ruin of Dirʿiyya
entries.hint: The mud-brick palace quarter of the First State's capital — the Salwā palace, the great mosque, the guest houses — was built up over seventy years, then deliberately dynamited by the Egyptians and left to melt. It is now a restored UNESCO World Heritage site.
entries.note: the at-Turaif district, UNESCO World Heritage since 2010; the Ad-Diriyah Gate Development Authority restoration.

entries.label: The Riyadh of the Second State
entries.hint: Turkī's new capital was a plainer thing — the first Qaṣr al-Ḥukm, a rebuilt town wall, and the al-Musmak fort with its battered walls and single iron-plated gate: a small, hard architecture for a state that had learned caution.
entries.note: King, 'The Traditional Architecture of Saudi Arabia' (1998); the al-Musmak fort, conventionally dated to c.1865.

entries.label: The suppression and the survival of the arts
entries.loc: the Saudi and Rashīdī towns of Najd
entries.hint: Strict Wahhābism banned instrumental music, representational art and the shrine crafts. What survived — and was even encouraged — was Nabaṭī war-poetry and the ʿarda, the men's sword-dance, which became a formal ceremony of both the Saudi and the Rashīdī courts.
entries.note: the traveller accounts of Najdi ceremony (Doughty, the Blunts); Lisa Urkevich, 'Music and Traditions of the Arabian Peninsula' (2015).

entries.label: The war qaṣīd and the court poets
entries.hint: The Nabaṭī poetry of the campaigns — celebrating a victory, mourning a defeat, carrying a challenge or a peace offer between amīrs — was the political speech of the emirates, and both the Saudi and the Rashīdī courts kept poets to compose it.
entries.note: Sowayan, 'Nabaṭi Poetry' (1985); Kurpershoek's editions of the poetry of the emirates.

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: The two foundational Najdi chronicles, the 19th-century European travellers, and the anti-Wahhābī counter-tradition the Saudi histories ignore

entries.label: Ibn Ghannām and Ibn Bishr
entries.hint: The two foundational Najdi histories: Ibn Ghannām's contemporary account of the movement (d. 1811) and Ibn Bishr's ʿUnwān al-majd (d. 1873), the great chronicle of both emirates. They are the Saudi state's own version of its origins, and the frame every later history argues with.
entries.note: Ḥusayn ibn Ghannām, Rawḍat al-afkar wa'l-afham; ʿUthmān ibn Bishr, ʿUnwan al-majd fi taʾrikh Najd.

entries.label: The European travellers
entries.hint: Burckhardt, Sadleir, Wallin, Palgrave, Pelly, Doughty and the Blunts crossed Najd in the 19th century and wrote it up for a Western public — a body of observation that is vivid, opinionated, sometimes fabricated, and the origin of the Western image of central Arabia.
entries.note: W. G. Palgrave, 'Narrative of a Year's Journey through Central and Eastern Arabia' (1865); Doughty (1888); Anne Blunt (1881); on Palgrave's unreliability, see the later scholarship.

entries.label: The counter-tradition
entries.hint: The anti-Wahhābī literature — Ottoman refutations, the Shiʿi accounts of Karbala, the Meccan and Cairene fatwās, the memoirs of the defeated — is a parallel historiography of the Saudi century that the Saudi chronicles never acknowledge.
entries.note: Ahmad Dallal, 'The Origins and Objectives of Islamic Revivalist Thought' (1993); Hala Fattah on the Ottoman-Iraqi reaction.

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: An economy of conquest and tribute, the growing merchant wealth of the Qaṣīm towns, the devastation of the Egyptian campaigns, and the interior briefly taxing the pearl coast

entries.label: Conquest and tribute as revenue
entries.hint: The First State's economy was expansion itself — the zakāt of newly submitted districts and the fifth of the plunder from raids on Iraq, the Hijaz and the Gulf. The Second State replaced plunder with steady tribute from the interior and the coast.
entries.note: Ibn Bishr; the fiscal analysis in ʿAbd al-Raḥīm ʿAbd al-Raḥmān; Winder (1965).

entries.label: The Qaṣīm merchant towns
entries.loc: ʿUnayzah and Buraydah, al-Qaṣīm, Saudi Arabia
entries.hint: ʿUnayzah and Buraydah grew into prosperous, semi-autonomous trading towns on the ʿUqaylāt caravan business — camels sold to the British-Indian and Egyptian armies, horses, and the transit trade between the Gulf, Iraq and the Hijaz.
entries.note: the ʿUqaylāt trade literature; Soraya Altorki and Donald Cole, 'Arabian Oasis City: The Transformation of ʿUnayzah' (1989).

entries.label: The devastation of the campaigns
entries.loc: al-Qaṣīm and Wadi Ḥanīfa, Saudi Arabia
entries.hint: Ibrāhīm Pasha's army cut down the palm groves of al-Qaṣīm and Wadi Ḥanīfa, razed towns and drove off the stock; the second Egyptian invasion did it again. The interior's thin agrarian economy took decades to recover each time.
entries.note: the Egyptian campaign accounts; Ibn Bishr on the destruction; Winder (1965).

entries.label: Tribute from the coasts
entries.loc: Riyadh · levied on the Gulf littoral
entries.hint: At its height under Fayṣal the Second State collected 'zakāt' from the Trucial shaykhs, Qatar and the Omani coast — the poor interior briefly taxing the pearl-rich littoral, a reversal of the usual direction of Arabian wealth that ended when Fayṣal died.
entries.note: Pelly's 1865 report; J. B. Kelly, 'Britain and the Persian Gulf 1795–1880' (1968).

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: The artillery that broke Dirʿiyya, the mud fort refined into something artillery-proof warfare could not take, and the rifle spreading into the interior

entries.label: Artillery and the fall of Dirʿiyya
entries.hint: The decisive technological gap of the Egyptian war was the cannon — Ibrāhīm Pasha's field and siege guns, served by French-trained crews, against mud walls and matchlocks. It is why a conscript army from Egypt could do what no Arabian power had ever done.
entries.note: the Egyptian campaign records; Khaled Fahmy, 'All the Pasha's Men' (1997), on Muḥammad ʿAlī's artillery.

entries.label: The mud fort perfected
entries.hint: The Second State and the Rashīdīs refined the earthen fortress — battered walls, split-palm gun-ports, a single iron-plated gate, an internal keep — into something that could hold against anything short of artillery, as ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz would prove at the Musmak in 1902.
entries.note: King, 'The Traditional Architecture of Saudi Arabia' (1998); the al-Musmak fort.

entries.label: The rifle reaches Najd
entries.loc: the interior, via the Gulf arms trade
entries.hint: Through the second half of the century the muzzle-loading and then breech-loading rifle spread into the interior through the Gulf arms trade, making the bedouin raid deadlier and slowly shifting the balance of force between the tribes and the walled towns.
entries.note: Kelly, 'Britain and the Persian Gulf' (1968), on the Gulf arms trade; the traveller accounts of Najdi weapons.

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: The Ottoman decision to send Egypt against the Saudis, Muḥammad ʿAlī's Arabian ambitions, British dealings with Fayṣal, the Rashīdī–Ottoman–Kuwaiti board of 1900, and the doctrine's spread abroad

entries.label: The Ottoman reaction
entries.hint: Karbala and the loss of the Ḥaramayn forced Istanbul to act, but the empire could not project power into Arabia itself. The sultan delegated the task to Muḥammad ʿAlī of Egypt — the arrangement that destroyed the First State.
entries.note: the Ottoman archives on the Arabian question; Fahmy, 'All the Pasha's Men' (1997).

entries.label: Muḥammad ʿAlī and Arabia
entries.hint: The Egyptian viceroy used the Arabian campaign to blood and expand his new army, secure the Hijaz revenue and the Red Sea, and press his own ambitions in the region — until the European powers forced him out of the Levant and Arabia in 1840.
entries.note: Fahmy (1997); the diplomacy of the 1840 Convention of London.

entries.label: Britain and the Second State
entries.hint: The British in the Gulf dealt with Fayṣal as the interior power — Pelly's mission to Riyadh in 1865, agreements over the coast tribute and the slave trade, and a settled policy of watching Najd closely without ever entering it.
entries.note: Pelly (1866); Kelly, 'Britain and the Persian Gulf 1795–1880' (1968).

entries.label: The Rashīdīs, the Ottomans and Kuwait
entries.hint: Muḥammad ibn Rashīd ruled Najd as an Ottoman client and drew Ottoman recognition and arms; the exiled Saudis were sheltered in Kuwait by Mubārak Āl Ṣabāḥ, himself playing the Ottomans against the British. It was the diplomatic board on which the reconquest of 1902 would be played.
entries.note: Al-Rasheed, 'Politics in an Arabian Oasis' (1991); the British Political Residency records for Kuwait.

entries.label: The daʿwa abroad
entries.hint: The Wahhābī doctrine spread beyond Arabia even as the state that produced it was destroyed — to India (where a hadith-revivalist movement was labelled 'Wahhabi' and prosecuted), through the pilgrims who carried it home from Mecca, and into the wider 19th-century current of Islamic reform.
entries.note: Dallal (1993) on the transnational reform current; the Indian 'Wahhabi trials' of the 1860s–70s.

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: The first pan-Arabian state since the Caliphate, its destruction as an Ottoman-Egyptian reassertion, a century of rise-and-fall, and the dynasty in Kuwait waiting for one more chance

entries.label: The first pan-Arabian state since the Caliphate
entries.hint: The First Saudi State was the first polity to rule most of the peninsula since the 7th century, and the first modern Islamic-revivalist state to actually hold power — a working template that the 20th century's Islamist movements would study closely.
entries.note: Al-Rasheed, 'A History of Saudi Arabia' (2010); the reception of the Saudi model in later Islamist thought.

entries.label: The Egyptian destruction and the Ottoman reassertion
entries.hint: The razing of Dirʿiyya was the Ottoman-Egyptian world re-imposing itself on an Arabia that had briefly slipped its grip. The Saudis absorbed the lesson: the Second State was built to survive, not to conquer.
entries.note: Winder (1965); Al-Rasheed (2010).

entries.label: The century of the two emirates
entries.hint: Two Saudi states rose and fell in Najd in a century and a half, each ended by an outside power or by its own succession wars. The pattern — expansion, overreach, collapse — is the one the third state would finally have to break.
entries.note: Kostiner and Al-Rasheed on the recurring pattern of Saudi state formation.

entries.label: The thread continues — Riyadh, 1902
entries.hint: The folio ends with Najd ruled from Ḥāʾil and the Āl Saʿūd as refugees in Kuwait. In January 1902 a young ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn Saʿūd will lead a small party over the wall of the Musmak fort and take Riyadh back — the start of the third and lasting Saudi state.
entries.note: a forward reference: saudi-1902-today (the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia from the recapture of Riyadh) is planned but not yet built.

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: The dynasty's women and children held in Cairo, slavery in the emirates, Lady Anne Blunt at the Rashīdī court, and the people driven out by a century of war

entries.label: The Saudi captivity in Cairo
entries.hint: After Dirʿiyya, the surviving Āl Saʿūd — women, children and princes including the future Fayṣal — were held in Cairo for a quarter-century, a dynasty living out its second exile in an Egyptian palace-prison until Fayṣal escaped in 1843.
entries.note: Winder (1965); the Egyptian records of the deported Saudi family.

entries.label: Slavery in the Saudi states
entries.hint: Enslaved Africans served in the amīrs' households and guards and worked the date estates; the trans-Arabian slave route ran through Najd from the Hijaz and the Gulf. British pressure on the traffic from mid-century met Saudi and Rashīdī resistance and had little effect inland.
entries.note: Kelly (1968) on the Gulf slave-trade agreements; Clarence-Smith, 'Islam and the Abolition of Slavery' (2006).

entries.label: Lady Anne Blunt at Ḥāʾil
entries.hint: The English traveller and horse-breeder reached the Rashīdī court in 1879 with her husband, wrote 'A Pilgrimage to Nejd', and carried Najdi mares back to found the Crabbet stud — one of very few women to leave a first-hand account of the interior, and a key figure in the global history of the Arabian horse.
entries.note: Anne Blunt, 'A Pilgrimage to Nejd' (1881); the Crabbet Arabian Stud records.

entries.label: The displaced of the campaigns
entries.loc: Najd · to the Gulf, Iraq and the diaspora
entries.hint: The Egyptian wars and the Saudi civil war drove waves of people out of the Najdi towns — to the Gulf ports, to Iraq, to the ʿUqaylāt merchant colonies. It was a recurring depopulation the interior's demography never fully recovered from.
entries.note: Winder (1965); Altorki and Cole, 'Arabian Oasis City' (1989), on ʿUnayzah's outward migration.
